claims.text: A short-time, high-energy surface treatment of a CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy alloy will refine its near-surface grains.
The proposed surface treatment will partially amorphize the near-surface material.
Laser shock peening or a friction-stir-based process can generate the proposed refined, partially amorphous surface state.
The treated surface will develop a stable, nanostructured tribofilm.
Nanograin boundaries and partially amorphized zones facilitate formation of a stable, self-replenishing tribofilm during sliding.
Frictional heating activates tribochemical reactions that form oxide or compound films at the sliding interface.
An oxide film formed during HEA sliding in air can reduce interfacial shear strength and coefficient of friction.
A nanocrystalline oxide glaze layer can provide solid lubrication and produce a gentler high-temperature wear regime.
The treatment-derived film will minimize adhesive wear across a broad temperature range.
The treatment will reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate by at least 30% relative to untreated alloy throughout 25–800 °C.
The tribofilm-mediated benefit will remain effective in air under loads typical of mechanical moving parts from 25 °C to approximately 800 °C.
Untreated CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy has a relatively coarse as-fabricated microstructure.
The untreated alloy does not reliably form or maintain a low-friction oxide layer during sliding.
At temperatures of at least 600 °C, adhesion and tribo-oxidation become important contributors to wear behavior.
In vacuum, insufficient oxygen may prevent maintenance of the protective tribofilm and eliminate its friction and wear benefits.
Exceeding the treatment's temperature or load thresholds may degrade the tribofilm and remove its benefits.
Long-term tribofilm durability over repeated thermal cycles and extended sliding distances has not been validated.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires at least a 30% reduction in both metrics at every temperature, but the falsification rule only rejects outcomes that are worse than or not significantly different from the control. A statistically significant improvement smaller than 30% would violate the prediction without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
